summary: Java is a platform-independent, object-oriented programming language that compiles source code into bytecode, which the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) then interprets and runs on any operating system.
shortNotes: Java was created by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems and released in 1995.
Java source files (.java) are compiled by javac into bytecode (.class files), not into machine code directly.
The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) reads bytecode and translates it into machine-specific instructions at runtime.
Write Once, Run Anywhere (WORA) means the same .class file runs on Windows, Linux, or macOS without changes.
The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) includes the JVM plus standard libraries; the JDK (Java Development Kit) includes the JRE plus the compiler and developer tools.
Java is strongly typed, meaning every variable must have a declared data type before use.

detailed.explanation:
Java is a high-level, class-based, object-oriented programming language designed to have as few implementation dependencies as possible. It was developed by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems (now owned by Oracle) and officially released in 1995. Java is one of the most widely used languages in the world, powering Android apps, enterprise web applications, and much more.

When you write a Java program, you save it as a `.java` file. The Java compiler (`javac`) then compiles this source code into **bytecode**, which is stored in a `.class` file. Bytecode is not machine code — it is an intermediate, platform-neutral instruction set that no physical processor understands directly.

This is where the **JVM (Java Virtual Machine)** comes in. The JVM is a software engine installed on your computer that reads the `.class` bytecode file and translates each instruction into the native machine code of your specific operating system and hardware. Because every major platform has its own JVM implementation, the same `.class` file runs everywhere — this is the famous **Write Once, Run Anywhere (WORA)** principle.

The three key components to understand are: the **JDK** (Java Development Kit), which you install when you want to write and compile Java programs; the **JRE** (Java Runtime Environment), which contains the JVM and standard libraries needed to run programs; and the **JVM** itself, which is the engine that executes bytecode. The JDK contains the JRE, and the JRE contains the JVM.

The JVM also handles important tasks like memory management through **Garbage Collection**, security checks, and just-in-time (JIT) compilation, where frequently executed bytecode is compiled directly to machine code for better performance.

definitions.meaning: A high-level, object-oriented, platform-independent programming language created by Sun Microsystems in 1995.
A software engine that executes Java bytecode by translating it into machine-specific instructions at runtime.
An intermediate, platform-neutral code generated by the Java compiler from .java source files, stored in .class files.
A full software package that includes the Java compiler (javac), JRE, and other developer tools needed to write and compile Java programs.
A subset of the JDK that includes the JVM and standard class libraries required to run Java programs but not to compile them.
Java's principle that compiled bytecode can run on any device or OS that has a compatible JVM installed, without recompilation.
An automatic memory management process in the JVM that frees memory occupied by objects that are no longer in use.
A component of the JVM that compiles frequently used bytecode into native machine code at runtime to improve performance.

points: Java source code (.java) → compiled by javac → bytecode (.class) → executed by JVM: remember this flow for exams.
The JVM is platform-specific (there is a different JVM for Windows, Linux, Mac), but the bytecode is platform-independent.
JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM: JDK contains JRE, JRE contains JVM. You need JDK to develop; JRE alone is enough to run.
Java is NOT compiled directly to machine code (unlike C or C++); this is what gives it platform independence.
The main class in a Java program must have the method: public static void main(String[] args) — this is the entry point.
Java is case-sensitive: 'Hello' and 'hello' are treated as different identifiers.
Garbage Collection happens automatically in Java; you do not need to manually free memory like in C.
The JIT compiler improves performance by converting hot (frequently run) bytecode into native machine code during execution.

codeExample.explanation:
Line 1-3: Comments explaining the file name and purpose. Java ignores these lines.
Line 5: We declare a public class named HelloJava. The file name must match the class name exactly.
Line 8: The main method — public static void main(String[] args) — is the entry point the JVM calls first when running the program.
Line 11: System.out.println prints a line of text to the console and moves to the next line.
Line 14: System.getProperty("java.version") asks the JVM for the current Java version at runtime; this shows that the JVM knows its environment.
Line 15: We print the version string with a label using the + operator to join strings.
Line 18-19: Similarly, os.name gives the operating system name, demonstrating WORA — the same bytecode prints a different OS name depending on where it runs.

commonMistakes: Naming the file differently from the public class name — for example, saving a class named 'HelloJava' in a file called 'hello.java' causes a compilation error because Java requires the file name and public class name to match exactly.

Confusing JDK, JRE, and JVM — students often think installing any one of them is enough for both writing and running programs; remember that to compile and run you need the JDK, while just running requires the JRE.

Thinking Java bytecode is machine code — bytecode is an intermediate format understood only by the JVM, not directly by your computer's processor; this misunderstanding causes confusion about why Java needs the JVM installed.

questions.prompt: What does the Java compiler (javac) produce when it compiles a .java source file?
questions.explanation: The javac compiler converts Java source code (.java) into bytecode stored in a .class file. This bytecode is platform-independent and is later interpreted by the JVM.

questions.prompt: Which component of the Java ecosystem is responsible for executing Java bytecode?
questions.explanation: The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) reads the .class bytecode file and translates its instructions into native machine code for the host operating system.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym WORA stand for in the context of Java?
questions.explanation: WORA — Write Once, Run Anywhere — means that Java bytecode compiled on one platform can run on any other platform that has a compatible JVM, without needing to recompile.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between JDK, JRE, and JVM?
options: JVM contains JRE which contains JDK
JRE contains JDK which contains JVM
JDK contains JRE which contains JVM
They are three separate, unrelated tools
questions.explanation: JDK is the largest package: it includes the JRE (plus compiler and tools). The JRE includes the JVM (plus standard libraries). So JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the correct entry point method signature that the JVM looks for to start a Java application?
questions.explanation: The JVM requires the method to be exactly: public static void main(String[] args). It must be public (accessible), static (no object needed), void (returns nothing), and take a String array as parameter.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler inside the JVM?
options: It compiles .java files into .class files before execution
It converts frequently used bytecode into native machine code at runtime for better performance
It automatically writes Java source code from requirements
It compresses .class files to save disk space
questions.explanation: The JIT compiler is a part of the JVM that identifies frequently executed bytecode (hot code) and compiles it into native machine code during runtime, speeding up execution significantly.

questions.prompt: Explain in your own words why Java is called a platform-independent language.
questions.answer: Java is platform-independent because the Java compiler converts source code into bytecode, which is not tied to any specific operating system or hardware. The JVM installed on each platform then translates this bytecode into the local machine's native instructions, so the same bytecode runs on Windows, Linux, or macOS without modification.
questions.explanation: The key insight is that it is the bytecode (not the source code) that travels across platforms, and each platform's JVM handles the translation to native machine code.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the JRE and the JDK? Which one should a student install to write and run Java programs?
questions.answer: The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) contains the JVM and standard libraries — it is only for running Java programs. The JDK (Java Development Kit) contains everything in the JRE plus the compiler (javac) and other developer tools. A student who wants to write and compile Java programs must install the JDK.
questions.explanation: End users who only need to run Java apps install the JRE. Developers must install the JDK because it includes the compiler needed to turn source code into bytecode.
System.out.println prints each argument on its own line. The first call prints the string Java and the second prints the integer 1995, each followed by a newline.

questions.prompt:
Write a Java program that prints the following three lines exactly:
Welcome to Java
Platform: Independent
Powered by JVM
questions.explanation: Each System.out.println() call prints one line of text to the console and automatically moves to the next line. The string argument passed inside the parentheses and double quotes is printed exactly as written. Three separate println calls produce three separate output lines.

steps.say: Hello everyone, welcome to your very first Java lesson. Today we are going to answer two big questions: what is Java, and how does it actually run on your computer?

write.content: What is Java and How the JVM Works

steps.say: Java is a programming language created by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems, and it was released in 1995. Today it powers everything from Android apps to large banking systems.
The most important feature of Java is that it is platform-independent, meaning code you write today can run on Windows, Linux, or Mac without any changes.
When you write a Java program, you save it as a dot-java file. Let us trace what happens next, step by step.
You then run the Java compiler, called javac, on that file. The compiler reads your source code and produces a dot-class file.
The dot-class file contains something called bytecode. Bytecode is not machine code — it is a special in-between language that no processor understands directly.
Think of bytecode as a universal language that every machine agrees to understand through a helper called the JVM.

scenes.title: The JVM – The Heart of Java

steps.say: Now here is the magic. Each operating system has its own version of the JVM, the Java Virtual Machine. It reads the bytecode and translates it into instructions your specific machine understands.
So the same dot-class file that runs on your Windows laptop also runs on your friend's Linux machine, because each has its own JVM that handles the translation.
This is the famous Write Once Run Anywhere principle. You write and compile once, and the JVM on each platform does the rest.
Students often get confused between three terms: JDK, JRE, and JVM. Let me draw this clearly for you.
The JVM is the engine that runs bytecode. The JRE is the JVM plus the standard libraries Java programs need.
The JDK is the full development kit. It includes the JRE plus the compiler and tools. As a student writing programs, always install the JDK.
Let us look at the simplest Java program so you can see the structure the JVM expects.
Every Java program needs a main method. This is the entry point — the first thing the JVM calls when it runs your program.
Inside main, we call System dot out dot println to print a message to the screen. Then we close both braces.
Great work today! Let us quickly recap what we learned.
Java source code is compiled by javac into bytecode, stored in a dot-class file.
The JVM on each platform reads that bytecode and runs it, giving us platform independence.

write.content: JVM runs bytecode on any platform

steps.say: And remember: install the JDK to develop, the JRE alone is only for running. See you in the next lesson!
